intro: An FDE engagement succeeds when the customer can run, use and improve what you built without you. Handoff is where many good projects quietly fail: the FDE moves to the next customer, knowledge leaves with them, the system drifts, and six months later nobody remembers how the integration works. This lesson covers planning handoff from the start, the documentation set that makes a system operable, enablement for users, operators and developers, defining ownership and support boundaries, and the follow-up that keeps the deployment healthy and growing.
objectives: Plan handoff from day one, with named customer owners for each area
Produce the documentation set: architecture, runbooks, configuration and decision records
Run enablement sessions for users, operators and developers with hands-on exercises
Define ownership, support tiers and escalation paths in writing
Measure handoff readiness and schedule follow-ups that sustain adoption

sections.heading: Plan handoff from the first week

blocks.text: Handoff is not a final-week activity. In the first week, ask who will own the system after you leave: who operates it, who supports users, who changes configuration, who decides on improvements. Involve those people throughout: let the future operator run the deployments with you, let the future admin change configuration while you watch. By the end, the handoff is a formality because they have already been doing the work.

rows: Deploy, upgrade, roll back and diagnose common failures alone
Answer common questions and route issues correctly
Change prompts, thresholds, access groups safely

items: **Overview**: what the system does, for whom, and the success metric it serves.
**Architecture**: the data-flow diagram from the security review, components, dependencies and where everything runs.
**Configuration reference**: every setting, its default, what changing it does, and who may change it.
**Runbooks**: step-by-step procedures for routine tasks and known failures.
**Decision records**: short notes on significant decisions and why they were made, so future maintainers do not undo them by accident.
**Contacts and support**: who owns what, how to reach your company, escalation paths.

blocks.caption: A runbook entry an on-call operator can follow at 3 a.m.
blocks.code:
RUNBOOK: Assistant answers 'I could not find this' for everything

Symptoms   Most questions return 'not found'; /readyz shows index: false
Impact     Users get no answers; handlers fall back to manual search
Check      1. kubectl get pods -n assistant (is the indexer CrashLooping?)
           2. kubectl logs deploy/assistant-indexer -n assistant --since=1h
           3. Look for 'SharePoint 401' (credential expired) or 'disk full'
Fix        401: rotate the SharePoint client secret in the vault, then
                kubectl rollout restart deploy/assistant-indexer -n assistant
           disk: expand PVC 'assistant-index' by 20Gi (see storage runbook)
Verify     /readyz index: true; ask 'What is the motor excess clause?'
Escalate   If not fixed in 60 min: vendor support, severity 2

blocks.text: Different people need different training. Keep sessions short, hands-on and recorded, and give every participant something to do, not just watch.

items: **Users**: a 30-minute session on doing their real work with the tool, what it is good and bad at, how to check its answers, and how to give feedback. Short guides and a few example tasks beat long manuals.
**Champions and admins**: configuration changes, access management, reading usage and quality dashboards, collecting feedback.
**Operators**: a game-day where they deploy, upgrade, roll back and fix two injected failures using only the runbooks while you observe silently.
**Developers** (if the customer will extend it): the codebase, the extension points, how to run tests and evaluations, and how to contribute.

blocks.text: The game-day is the most reliable readiness test. If operators cannot recover from a failure using the runbook while you sit on your hands, the runbook or the training is not finished.

Write down who does what after go-live. A common model has three tiers: the customer's service desk handles first-line questions; the customer's platform team handles operations using runbooks; your company's support handles product defects and escalations under the support agreement. Define severity levels, response times, how to open a case, and what information to include (the support bundle). Ambiguity here produces either angry customers or an FDE who never really leaves.

items: **Readiness checklist** signed off by each customer owner: docs reviewed, game-day passed, access transferred, monitoring and alerts routed to them.
**Access cleanup**: remove your accounts and credentials, rotate any secrets you handled, confirm in writing.
**Data cleanup**: delete any copies of customer data you held, as agreed in the access request.
**Follow-up cadence**: check-ins at two weeks, six weeks and three months reviewing adoption, quality, incidents and the next use case.
**Retrospective** with your own team: what to add to templates, playbooks and the product.

blocks.text: Follow-ups are not just courtesy. Adoption often drops after the FDE leaves; catching it early, with fresh training or a small fix, protects the outcome you worked for, and the three-month review is usually where the next engagement starts.

practice.title: Hand over a system you built
steps: Pick one project from this track and write the full documentation set: overview, architecture, configuration reference, three runbooks, two decision records, contacts.
Run a 30-minute user session for a friend acting as a user, with three real tasks.
Run a game-day: a friend acting as operator must deploy, upgrade, roll back and fix two failures you inject, using only your runbooks.
Improve every runbook step where they got stuck.
Write a support model: tiers, severities, response times and how to open a case with a support bundle.
Write the readiness checklist and a follow-up plan for two weeks, six weeks and three months.

focus: Name customer owners in week one and involve them throughout.
Docs: overview, architecture, config reference, runbooks, decision records, contacts.
Enablement per audience; hands-on and recorded.
Game-day with runbooks only is the readiness test.
Write down support tiers, severities and escalation.
Clean up access and data; follow up at 2 weeks, 6 weeks and 3 months.

items.desc: How it shows up and who is affected
Exact commands and what to look for

pitfalls: Starting handoff in the final week.
Documentation that describes the code but not how to operate it.
Training by demonstration only, with no hands-on practice.
Alerts still routed to the FDE after go-live.
Leaving with active credentials and copies of customer data.

quiz.q: What is the most reliable test that operators are ready to own the system?
options: A game-day using only the runbooks
A slide presentation of the architecture
A signed acknowledgement that they read the docs
A survey asking whether they feel confident
quiz.explain: Recovering from real injected failures without help proves the runbooks and training work; reading and slides do not.

quiz.q: When should you identify who will own the system after you leave?
options: In the first week of the engagement
In the final week, before the handoff meeting
After go-live, once support tickets arrive
Only if the customer asks about it
quiz.explain: Early owners can shadow and then lead the work, so the handoff happens gradually rather than as a cliff edge.

quiz.q: Why include decision records in the documentation?
options: So maintainers know why choices were made
Because auditors require every code change documented
To prove the FDE worked enough hours
To replace the need for runbooks
quiz.explain: Without the reasoning, a later team may reverse a deliberate choice, such as a security constraint, and reintroduce a solved problem.

quiz.q: Alerts for the deployed system still page the FDE two months after go-live. What does this indicate?
options: Handoff is incomplete: ownership was not transferred
The FDE is doing an excellent job
The system needs more alerts configured
The customer simply prefers it this way
quiz.explain: Ownership includes being paged; until alerts route to the customer's operators, they do not truly own the system.

options: Adoption can drop after you leave
Contracts always require monthly meetings
To keep billing hours on the account
Because the software needs weekly manual restarts
quiz.explain: Check-ins catch falling usage or quality early and often surface the next use case.
